title: Pointers as Parameters
summary: C++ passes arguments by copying them, so a function cannot change the caller's variables, unless it receives their addresses. Out-parameters, swap, returning several results, optional parameters with nullptr, and when a reference is the better choice.
markdown:
## Functions get copies

When you call a function, each argument is **copied** into the function's parameter. Changing the parameter changes the copy:

```cpp
#include <iostream>

void heal(int health)
{
    health += 25;          // changes the local copy only
}

int main()
{
    int health{ 50 };
    heal(health);
    std::cout << health << '\n';   // still 50
}
```

The `health` inside `heal` is a separate variable in `heal`'s stack frame (lesson 4.02 shows the frames). It vanishes when the function returns.

```demo-stack
title: heal gets a copy
call main | main starts with its own health.
local health = 50
call heal health=50 | heal gets a new frame with a COPY of the value.
set health = 75 | Only the copy changes.
return | heal's frame, and the copy, are gone.
return 0 | main's health is still 50.
```

## Passing the address

If the function receives the **address** instead, it can reach the caller's variable:

```cpp
#include <iostream>

void heal(int* health)
{
    *health += 25;         // follow the address to the caller's variable
}

int main()
{
    int health{ 50 };
    heal(&health);          // pass where health is, not what it is
    std::cout << health << '\n';   // 75
}
```

The pointer is still copied, but a copy of an address points at the same place. This is how C, and lots of Windows API functions, let a function change things in its caller.

## The classic: swap

```cpp
#include <iostream>

void swapInts(int* a, int* b)
{
    const int old{ *a };
    *a = *b;
    *b = old;
}

int main()
{
    int left{ 1 }, right{ 2 };
    swapInts(&left, &right);
    std::cout << left << ' ' << right << '\n';   // 2 1
}
```

Without pointers (or references) `swap` cannot be written at all.

## Out-parameters

A function returns one value, but sometimes it has several results. A common pattern returns success or failure and writes the results through pointers, called **out-parameters**:

```cpp-norun
// Splits "12:45" into hours and minutes. Returns false if the text is not a time.
bool parseTime(const std::string& text, int* hours, int* minutes);

int h{}, m{};
if (parseTime("12:45", &h, &m)) { /* use h and m */ }
```

The Windows API is full of these: `GetExitCodeProcess(process, &exitCode)` returns success as a `BOOL` and the exit code through a pointer. Modern C++ often prefers returning a struct or a `std::optional`, but you will read out-parameters constantly.

## Optional parameters

A pointer parameter can be `nullptr`, which gives a natural way to say "I do not want this result":

```cpp-norun
void stats(const int* values, int count, int* minOut, int* maxOut)
{
    // ... work out lo and hi ...
    if (minOut) *minOut = lo;     // the caller may not want the minimum
    if (maxOut) *maxOut = hi;
}

stats(data, 10, nullptr, &largest);   // only interested in the maximum
```

The rule that follows: **if a parameter may be nullptr, check before writing through it**. If it may not, say so in the function's comment, or better, use a reference.

## References: pointers that cannot be null

A C++ **reference** (`int&`) is an address too, under the hood, but with three differences: it must be bound to an object when created, it can never be re-pointed, and it cannot be null. You use it without `*` or `&`:

```cpp-norun
void heal(int& health) { health += 25; }
heal(health);   // no & at the call
```

So which to use?

| Use | When |
|---|---|
| `T&` | the function always needs an object to change |
| `const T&` | the function only reads a large object and wants to avoid a copy |
| `T*` | "no object" is a valid answer (nullptr), or the code talks to a C API |
| `const T*` | the same, read only |

This course uses pointers almost everywhere, because pointers are the subject. In your own C++ code, prefer references when null is not meaningful.

## Check yourself
```quiz
? Why does `void heal(int h) { h += 25; }` not change the caller's variable?
- `+=` does not work on parameters
+ The argument is copied into `h`; the function changes its copy, which disappears when it returns
- The caller's variable is `const` inside a function call
- The change is made, but only becomes visible after the next call
> C++ passes arguments by value. To change the caller's variable the function needs its address (a pointer) or a reference.

? `heal(int* h)` is called with `heal(&health)`. Is the pointer copied?
- No, pointers are always passed by reference
- No, `&health` passes `health` itself rather than a copy
- Yes, and so `*h` changes only a copy of `health`
+ Yes, but the copy holds the same address, so `*h` reaches the caller's `health`
> Every argument is copied, pointers included. A copy of an address still leads to the same object.

? When is a pointer parameter better than a reference parameter?
- Whenever the function needs to change the caller's variable
- When the object is large, because pointers are faster than references
+ When "no object" is meaningful and the caller may pass `nullptr`, or for a C-style interface
- When the function must not change the object
> A reference can also change the caller's object and is no slower. A pointer earns its place when null is a valid "not given", or when the interface must be callable from C.

? A function writes `*countOut = n;` and the documentation says `countOut` is optional. What is missing?
- A cast of `n` to `int*` before the assignment
+ A null check: `if (countOut) *countOut = n;`
- An `&` in front of `countOut`
- A `delete countOut;` at the end of the function
> Optional means the caller may pass `nullptr`, and writing through `nullptr` crashes. Check before you write.
```

cards.a:
The argument is copied into `h`; the function changes its copy, which disappears when it returns

cards.q: A function writes `*countOut = n;` and the documentation says `countOut` is optional. What is missing?
cards.a:
A null check: `if (countOut) *countOut = n;`
